title: The stones would shout (Luke 19:28–40)
hookLine: if these were silent, the stones would cry out

lines: DOWN FROM THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.
cards: Palm Sunday. Most people picture crowds waving palm branches, children shouting hosanna. Now open Luke.
No palms. No hosanna. John has the palms; Matthew and Mark have branches and hosannas.
Luke's version is quieter in some ways and louder in others. He tells it from just over the Mount of Olives, on the road down into Jerusalem, and by the end even the rocks by the road are in on it.

teach.h: A COLT, AND CLOAKS ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: Jesus sends two disciples for a colt, in the King James Bible "whereon yet never man sat." They throw their cloaks on it, and as he rides, people spread their clothes on the road. Cloaks, not palms.
An old story in Kings has people spreading their garments under a new king's feet. And the prophet Zechariah had pictured Jerusalem's king coming humbly, riding on a colt.

As the road starts down the Mount of Olives and the city comes into view, "the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen."
They sing: "Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest."
That echoes the angels at his birth: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace. The angels sang it to shepherds at the start; now his followers sing it back as he comes to the city.
Then some Pharisees say: "Master, rebuke thy disciples." Maybe they're worried the Romans will hear the word king.

teach.h: THE STONES WOULD IMMEDIATELY CRY OUT.
teach.b: Jesus answers: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out." It may echo Habakkuk, where "the stone shall cry out of the wall." There, the stones accuse injustice.
Here, they'd praise. Some praise is too true to be silenced; if people won't say it, creation will.

how: On Palm Sunday, many churches hold a procession with palm branches, drawing on John's Gospel, and in years when Luke is read, the reading tells of cloaks on the road and the stones that would cry out.

o: you're right. this could bring trouble.

games.why: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out."

practice: Think of something good you've seen lately, one of Luke's mighty works, large or small: a recovery, a kindness, a sunrise, a job well done. Then say it out loud in a normal voice, even alone: thank you for this, this was good.
If you pray, praise God aloud for it, and then sit in the quiet that follows.
